headline: US and Iran reignite their war over the Strait of Hormuz: Trump drops a 20% shipping fee but presses a naval blockade as strikes fly, pushing oil to a one-month high.
the_big_picture: The single thread running through today is the re-escalation of the US-Iran conflict at the Strait of Hormuz, the chokepoint that carries roughly a fifth of the world's oil. Trump backed off a threatened 20% transit fee but is pushing ahead with a naval blockade while both sides trade strikes and tankers come under attack, sending crude to a one-month high. That oil spike is the hinge for everything downstream: US inflation cooled to 3.5% but officials flagged fresh upside risk, India's inflation just breached its central bank's target, the rupee slid past 96 and the Sensex fell. Running underneath, an AI storyline cuts both ways: IBM shed roughly $70bn in a day after stumbling on AI deals, even as China's AI-driven exports jumped 27% and Nvidia began shipping powerful H200 chips into China.

stories.title: A data center operator is exploring a $100 billion IPO — a sign of how big the AI building boom has gotten
key_points: **Vantage Data Centers** is exploring an IPO that could value it at roughly **$100 billion**, which would make it the largest data-center listing ever
The company, backed by private equity firm **Silver Lake** and infrastructure investor **DigitalBridge**, could raise around **$10 billion** in the offering
A **sale**, including a partial stake sale, is also being considered as an alternative to going public
Talks are still preliminary — no formal process has launched, and timing, size, and structure could all change
Vantage has already raised roughly **$11 billion** since late 2023 to build out data centers, underscoring how much capital the AI infrastructure race is consuming
stories.background: **Data centers** are the physical warehouses full of servers and specialized chips (like Nvidia's GPUs) that actually run AI models — every ChatGPT-style answer or AI image is computed inside one. As AI demand has exploded, so has the need for these facilities, and the private equity and infrastructure firms that own them have been pouring in tens of billions of dollars to build bigger ones, faster. Vantage Data Centers is one of the largest such operators globally, and its owners — Silver Lake and DigitalBridge — have already put in over **$9 billion** in equity since 2023 to fund its expansion.
stories.what_happened: According to people familiar with the matter, **Vantage Data Centers** has held preliminary discussions in recent weeks about possible exit paths for its private-equity owners, meeting informally with financial advisers about a stock market listing or a sale. An **IPO** could value the company at around **$100 billion** and raise roughly **$10 billion** for the business — a figure that would make it the largest-ever data center IPO. The company is also weighing a sale, including selling a stake to new investors, as an alternative route. Any deal remains at an early, non-binding stage, and could happen as soon as next year if it proceeds. The exploration comes as AI-driven demand for computing power keeps pushing valuations for data-center operators sharply higher.
stories.why_it_matters: A single company's IPO discussions might sound like a niche financial story, but the **scale here is the point**: a $100 billion valuation for a company that essentially just owns buildings full of servers shows how much investors believe the AI boom will keep driving demand for computing power. It's also a signal that the earliest AI infrastructure investors are now looking for ways to cash out some of their winnings.
stories.ripple_effects: If Vantage goes public at anywhere near this valuation, it will likely encourage other data-center operators and AI infrastructure owners to pursue similar listings, funneling even more capital into building AI computing capacity — including in countries like India, which is racing to build its own AI data-center hubs. It also gives ordinary stock market investors a new, direct way to bet on the AI boom without buying shares of the AI companies themselves.
stories.why_now: AI companies' hunger for computing capacity has been rising all year, pushing up what investors are willing to pay for the physical infrastructure that powers AI — making this a good window for early backers to consider cashing out at a high valuation.
stories.watch_next: Whether Vantage formally files for an IPO or opts for a sale instead, and whether other large private data-center operators follow with their own listings.

key_terms.definition: The first time a private company sells shares to the public on a stock exchange, letting anyone buy a piece of it.
A large facility packed with computer servers and chips that stores data and runs computing tasks — including the calculations behind AI models.

stories.the_lesson: When a boom is real, it shows up not just in the prices of the flashy companies at the center of it, but in the unglamorous infrastructure — pipes, warehouses, power plants — that the boom depends on; watching what that infrastructure is worth is often a clearer signal than watching the hype.
stories.market_link: Signals continued strong valuations for AI infrastructure and data-center REITs/operators broadly; an eventual IPO would be one of the largest tech listings in years.

stories.title: US inflation cools slightly in July, but the Fed still isn't ready to cut rates
key_points: Headline US consumer prices rose just **0.1%** in July, holding the annual inflation rate at **3.4%**
**Core inflation** (which strips out food and energy) rose 0.2% for the month; its annual rate eased to **2.5%**
**Shelter costs** — rent and housing — drove roughly two-thirds of July's price increase on their own
Energy prices fell **1.5%** in July, cushioning the headline number after a 5.7% drop in June
Wall Street read it as good-but-not-great news: the **S&P 500** and Nasdaq both edged higher, but traders still see little chance of a Fed rate cut this year
stories.background: The US Federal Reserve targets **2% annual inflation** as the sweet spot for a healthy economy — enough price growth to signal demand, not so much that it erodes paychecks. Since 2025, inflation has stayed stubbornly above that target, kept elevated by tariffs on imported goods, high shelter costs, and a resilient job market that keeps consumer spending strong. The monthly **Consumer Price Index (CPI)**, published by the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, is the single most-watched number for figuring out what the Fed will do next with interest rates — the cost of borrowing money that ripples through mortgages, credit cards, and business loans worldwide.
stories.what_happened: The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported on **August 12** that the Consumer Price Index rose **0.1%** in July after actually falling 0.4% in June, a reversal that still left the **annual rate at 3.4%**, down slightly from the prior month. Core CPI — the Fed's preferred gauge because it excludes volatile food and energy prices — climbed 0.2% for the month, with its annual pace **easing to 2.5%**. Shelter, which makes up roughly a third of the entire index, rose 0.1% and alone accounted for about two-thirds of July's overall increase. Energy prices provided relief, dropping 1.5% after a steep 5.7% fall in June. Markets initially cheered the report as evidence inflation isn't reaccelerating: the S&P 500 climbed about 0.26% to close at 7,748.50 and the Nasdaq Composite rose 0.54% to 26,588.49, helped along by AI-linked stocks. But traders' bets on a Fed rate cut in September stayed muted, since inflation remains well above the 2% target.
stories.why_it_matters: This is the closest thing to a monthly report card on whether the Fed can start cutting interest rates without reigniting inflation. A cooler number keeps hope alive for cheaper borrowing later this year; a hot one would push relief further away. Because the US dollar and US interest rates are the reference point for global finance, this single report moves stock markets, currencies, and bond yields **everywhere**, not just in America.
stories.ripple_effects: Lower US rates eventually mean a weaker dollar and cheaper borrowing costs globally, which tends to pull investment money toward emerging markets like India — part of why Indian benchmark indices opened higher on the back of this data. Conversely, if the Fed stays on hold for longer, the dollar tends to stay strong, making imports (like crude oil, which India buys heavily) costlier for countries whose currencies weaken against it. Rate-sensitive sectors — technology, real estate, and highly-indebted companies — are the most immediately exposed to whatever the Fed decides next.
stories.why_now: This is the regular monthly CPI release, but it carries extra weight because it's one of the last major inflation readings before the Fed's **September policy meeting**, where officials will decide whether to hold or cut interest rates.
stories.watch_next: The Fed's September FOMC meeting, where officials will weigh this data alongside the next jobs report before deciding on rates.

key_terms.definition: A monthly US government measure of how much prices for a broad basket of everyday goods and services have changed — the main gauge of inflation.
Inflation with food and energy prices stripped out, because those swing a lot month to month and can hide the underlying trend.

stories.the_lesson: A single monthly data point can move trillions of dollars in markets not because of the number itself, but because of what it implies about the price of borrowing money everywhere — interest rates are the gravity that everything else in finance orbits around.
stories.market_link: Directly moves US Treasury yields, the dollar, and rate-sensitive sectors like tech and real estate; also lifted sentiment on Indian markets (Sensex, Nifty) which opened higher partly on this data.

stories.title: Putin threatens to seize European ships 'anywhere' in retaliation for EU moves against Russia's sanctioned 'shadow fleet'
key_points: Putin called EU plans to sell off cargo from seized Russian tankers **'piracy and banditry'** and vowed to **'respond in kind'**.
He said Russia would seize European ships **wherever it 'deems necessary'** — explicitly including the **Pacific**, far from European waters.
The threat responds to new EU sanctions letting member states **sell the oil and cargo** from detained 'shadow fleet' tankers.
**Nine** such tankers have been detained in Europe since the start of 2026, **four of them in France**.
Putin made the comments while personally overseeing **Russian naval drills** in the Far East.
stories.background: Russia's 'shadow fleet' is a network of aging, often unregistered or falsely-flagged oil tankers that Moscow uses to keep exporting oil despite Western **sanctions** imposed after its invasion of Ukraine — sanctions being economic penalties, like trade or financial restrictions, meant to pressure a country's government. European countries have increasingly intercepted and detained these tankers, several of them linked to sanctioned Russian companies or suspected of sabotage, like the tanker that sank off Oman spilling oil across protected coastline. Last month the EU passed new rules letting member states go a step further: not just detain the ships, but actually sell their oil and cargo.
stories.what_happened: President Vladimir Putin said Wednesday that Russia would seize European ships in retaliation if EU countries follow through on selling off cargo from detained Russian 'shadow fleet' tankers. Speaking while overseeing **naval drills in Russia's Far East**, Putin called the EU's sanctions move **'piracy and banditry'** and said, **'We will be forced to respond in kind.'** He specified the retaliation would not necessarily target ships in the same waters where Russian vessels were seized — Russia would act **'anywhere, including in the area of responsibility of the Pacific Fleet.'** The trigger was a new EU sanctions package passed last month permitting member states to sell the oil or cargo seized from shadow-fleet tankers; **nine** such tankers have been detained across Europe since the start of 2026, **four of them by France** alone.
stories.why_it_matters: This is a direct escalation from sanctions-and-detentions into a threat of retaliatory seizures of commercial shipping — a step that, if carried out, would raise real risk for any European-flagged or European-owned vessel operating near Russian-controlled waters, including far from Europe itself.
stories.ripple_effects: Shipping insurers may raise premiums or add exclusions for vessels transiting near Russian naval zones, especially in the Pacific and Arctic. European shipping and logistics firms could face new operational risk calculations, and the EU may pause or slow-walk the cargo-sale plan to avoid provoking retaliation. It also adds another flashpoint to an already tense standoff that includes the Ukraine war, Baltic Sea cable sabotage allegations, and NATO's hybrid-warfare warnings.
stories.why_now: The threat comes right as EU states move from simply detaining shadow-fleet tankers to actually selling their cargo — the first time sanctions enforcement has crossed into taking Russian-linked assets, which Moscow is treating as a new redline.
stories.watch_next: Whether any EU state actually completes a cargo sale from a detained tanker — that would be the trigger point for Putin to test his retaliation threat.

key_terms.definition: A network of aging, often unregistered oil tankers Russia uses to export oil while evading Western sanctions.
Economic penalties, like trade or financial restrictions, that governments impose on a country to pressure its behavior.

stories.the_lesson: Sanctions enforcement tends to escalate in steps — freezing assets, then detaining them, then selling them — and each step invites a proportional response from the country being sanctioned, so tracking the exact stage of enforcement matters as much as tracking the sanctions themselves.
stories.market_link: Rising Russia-EU shipping tensions could push up marine insurance costs and add a geopolitical risk premium to Brent crude and European energy prices.

stories.title: Spain just had its first total solar eclipse since 1905 — and it's only the opener in an unheard-of three-eclipse run through 2028

thread.previously: We covered Tuesday's eclipse as it happened: totality began around 15:34 GMT and swept from Iceland to Spain, lasting up to 2 minutes 18 seconds, watched by an estimated 15 million people, and coinciding with the Perseid meteor shower.
thread.changed: Now that the event has passed, the bigger story is emerging: this wasn't a one-off. It's the first of **three consecutive total or annular solar eclipses to cross Spain by 2028** — a concentration of eclipses astronomers say almost no country has ever seen in such a short span, turning Spain into a hub for eclipse tourism for the rest of the decade.

key_points: Monday's eclipse was Spain's first total solar eclipse in mainland territory since **1905** — 121 years.
A second total eclipse will cross Spain again on **August 2, 2027**, visible from the Iberian Peninsula down into North Africa and the Middle East.
A third eclipse — an **annular** ('ring of fire') eclipse where the Moon doesn't fully cover the Sun — follows on **January 26, 2028**.
Astronomers are calling it the **'Iberian trio'**, an occurrence so rare that few countries have experienced three eclipses this close together.
The totality path this week reached as far as **Palma, Valencia, Zaragoza, Bilbao and León**, with observers getting up to 1 minute 50 seconds of darkness.
stories.background: Total solar eclipses happen somewhere on Earth every year or two, but any single spot on the planet typically waits **centuries** between them, because the Moon's shadow is only about 100 miles wide and sweeps across a thin, fast-moving path. Mainland Spain's last one was in **1905**; mainland Europe as a whole hadn't seen one since **1999**. That's what made this week's event, and the discovery that two more are coming within two years, so unusual to scientists who track these cycles.
stories.what_happened: On Wednesday, the Moon's shadow swept from **Greenland and Iceland across northern Spain** as the Sun set, delivering totality — the brief window when the Moon fully blocks the Sun — to an estimated **15 million people**, most of them in Spain. It was the **first total solar eclipse over mainland Europe since 1999** and mainland Spain's first since **1905**. Scientists used the rare darkness to study the Sun's **corona**, the outer atmosphere normally invisible in daylight, which affects space weather that can disrupt satellites and power grids. What makes this moment bigger than a single afternoon is the calendar that follows: Spain will see a second total eclipse on **August 2, 2027**, then an annular eclipse on **January 26, 2028** — a three-eclipse sequence astronomers are calling the 'Iberian trio', the first cluster of total eclipses over mainland Europe this century.
stories.why_it_matters: A single total eclipse over a populated country is already rare; three in under two years is close to unprecedented, and it's turning Spain into the epicenter of global eclipse tourism through 2028, with real economic upside for towns along the path. It's also a live science opportunity — each eclipse gives researchers a fresh, brief window to study the Sun's corona and its effects on Earth's technology.
stories.ripple_effects: Expect a tourism boom in the towns along each path of totality, similar to what small US towns saw during the 2017 and 2024 American eclipses — hotel bookings, festivals, and traffic crushes. Airlines and observatories are already building special viewing flights and expeditions around the 2027 and 2028 dates. Spain's astronomy and tourism agencies are likely to promote the country as an eclipse-chasing destination for the rest of the decade.
stories.why_now: The Iberian trio is surfacing today because Wednesday's eclipse — the first of the three — just happened, prompting scientists and outlets to explain the full three-eclipse sequence for the first time to a mainstream audience.
stories.watch_next: Mark August 2, 2027 — the second total eclipse in the sequence, visible across Spain, North Africa and parts of the Middle East.

key_terms.definition: The brief period during a total eclipse when the Moon completely covers the Sun's disk and the sky goes dark in daytime.
An eclipse where the Moon is slightly too far from Earth to fully cover the Sun, leaving a bright ring ('ring of fire') visible around it.
The Sun's outer atmosphere, normally invisible in daylight but visible as a glowing halo during a total eclipse.

stories.the_lesson: Rare astronomical alignments cluster in ways that feel like coincidence but are just orbital mechanics repeating on a predictable cycle — once you know the pattern, you can plan years ahead for events that seem like once-in-a-lifetime luck.
stories.market_link: Spanish tourism, hospitality, and regional airline stocks could see a multi-year demand bump from eclipse tourism through 2028.

stories.title: Russia releases US Marine veteran Robert Gilman after nearly four years in detention, on Trump's personal appeal to Putin
key_points: **Robert Gilman**, a 32-year-old former US Marine, has been released from Russian detention and has returned to the United States.
He was held since **2022** on disputed charges of beating a police officer after being pulled off a train for causing a disturbance.
His family and advocates say he was tortured, and was in a **'dissociative stupor' for 47 days** before being moved to a hospital.
President **Trump personally raised the case with Putin**, and says Russia asked for **nothing in return** — no prisoner swap took place.
Gilman is headed to a **US military hospital in Texas** for medical and psychological assessment.
stories.background: Gilman was detained in Russia in 2022, one of a number of Americans caught up in Russian legal proceedings since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine began that year. Such cases have often become bargaining chips: past releases, like the 2024 multi-country prisoner exchange, involved Russia swapping detained Americans for Russians held in Western countries. Gilman's family and legal advocates have spent years arguing his charges were disputed and that he was being mistreated in custody, warning at points that he was near death.
stories.what_happened: Russia released Gilman on what officials describe as humanitarian grounds, and he has now arrived back in the United States. His advocates say that before his release he had been in a dissociative stupor for 47 days as a result of alleged physical and psychological abuse in custody, and had to be moved to a hospital, hooked to a feeding tube and handcuffed to a bed. Trump said he personally discussed the case with Vladimir Putin and that Russia agreed to free Gilman without asking for anyone in return — a departure from the more typical prisoner-swap pattern seen in past releases. Gilman is now traveling to a US military hospital in Texas, where he'll undergo medical and psychological evaluation before any further treatment.
stories.why_it_matters: A no-strings-attached release is unusual in the current climate between Washington and Moscow, where prisoner cases are usually tied to broader negotiations. It suggests at least one narrow channel of direct, personal diplomacy between Trump and Putin is still functioning even as the two countries remain at odds over the war in Ukraine.
stories.ripple_effects: The release may raise hopes for other American families with relatives detained in Russia, who will likely point to this case as evidence that direct presidential appeals can work. It could also feed into the broader, tense backdrop of US-Russia relations, where issues like Ukraine, sanctions and the Strait of Hormuz standoff remain unresolved.
stories.why_now: The release comes as Trump and Putin have had recent direct contact on other fronts, including the Ukraine war, suggesting this case was raised as part of that broader channel of communication.
stories.watch_next: Whether Gilman's medical assessment in Texas reveals the full extent of his treatment in custody, and whether other detained Americans in Russia see similar movement.
stories.the_lesson: Even when two governments are in open conflict over major issues, narrow humanitarian channels — often driven by direct, personal appeals between leaders — can still produce results where broader diplomacy has stalled.

stories.title: Colombia's earthquake toll climbs past 265 as more than 2,700 remain reported missing
key_points: The confirmed death toll from Monday's **7.4-magnitude earthquake** has climbed past **265**, up from the 220-227 range reported a day earlier.
Volunteer networks tracking family reports say more than **2,700 people are still unaccounted for**, far above the government's own missing-persons count.
Rescue teams have recorded more than **70 aftershocks** and are using **thermal-imaging drones and cadaver dogs** to search collapsed buildings in Cali.
More than **1,100 homes have been destroyed** and **8,300 damaged**, with roads into the epicenter near San José del Palmar still blocked.
Dramatic rescues continue even past the 72-hour survival window — including a **baby pulled alive from a collapsed Cali apartment block**.
stories.background: A **7.4-magnitude earthquake** struck Colombia's Pacific coast on Monday, the strongest the country has recorded in a decade. It hit hardest in the western Chocó region, near the town of San José del Palmar, and shook the capital Bogotá and the city of Cali. The disaster is the **first major crisis test** for Colombia's new president, Abelardo de la Espriella, whose government initially limited international rescue offers to just four countries — a decision now under public criticism as the scale of the damage has become clearer.
stories.what_happened: As of Wednesday, Colombian authorities had confirmed at least **265 dead**, a sharp rise from the 220-227 figures reported the previous day, with officials warning the number will likely keep climbing as rescuers reach areas still cut off by blocked roads. Separately, volunteer-run tracking databases — which count family reports the government hasn't yet verified — put the number of people still unaccounted for at **more than 2,700**. Rescue crews have logged over **70 aftershocks** since the initial quake and are using thermal-imaging drones, cadaver dogs and specialized rubble-clearing equipment to keep searching in Cali, where a woman was pulled alive from debris almost 30 hours after the quake and a baby was rescued from a collapsed apartment building. The material toll is also severe: more than **1,100 homes destroyed** and **8,300 more damaged** across the affected region. Colombia had initially asked for help from only the US, El Salvador, Ecuador and Israel, but has since widened its request, with Peru now confirming it will send volunteer rescuers too.
stories.why_it_matters: The rising toll shows how much the true scale of a disaster can be underestimated in its first 48 hours, especially when roads to the hardest-hit areas are blocked. It's also becoming a defining early test of the new Colombian government's crisis-management credibility, after criticism that it was too slow and too narrow in asking the world for help.
stories.ripple_effects: Colombia's government faces mounting domestic pressure to accept more international assistance and speed up aid distribution, especially to remote Chocó communities. The scale of destroyed housing points to a long, expensive rebuilding effort that will strain public finances, and insurers operating in the region are likely to face a wave of claims.
stories.why_now: The toll is climbing today specifically because rescue teams are only now reaching previously blocked roads into the epicenter, and because volunteer networks are cross-referencing missing-persons reports that the government hasn't yet verified.
stories.watch_next: Whether Colombia formally widens its request for international rescue and reconstruction aid beyond the current handful of countries.

key_terms.definition: The rough period after a disaster like an earthquake during which the odds of finding people alive in rubble drop sharply — after which rescue efforts increasingly shift toward recovery.

stories.the_lesson: Official death tolls after a disaster are almost always undercounts in the first days — the real scale only emerges once rescuers physically reach every blocked-off area and volunteer networks catch missing-persons reports the government hasn't yet verified.

thread.previously: Yesterday we reported the confirmed death toll had passed 220-227, the critical 72-hour survival window had effectively closed, and Colombia's government was facing backlash for initially limiting foreign rescue offers to just four countries.
thread.changed: The confirmed toll has now climbed past 265, volunteer networks report more than 2,700 people still unaccounted for, and rescuers using thermal drones and dog teams have kept pulling survivors — including a baby — from the rubble in Cali even after the survival window closed.

stories.title: A sanctioned Russian 'shadow fleet' tanker sinking off Oman has spread oil across roughly 800 square kilometers of protected coastline
key_points: The **Caroline Bezengi**, a sanctioned tanker in Russia's "shadow fleet," is sinking after an unexplained explosion in **June**.
It was carrying almost **1 million barrels** of Russian crude bound for Asia when it first reported trouble.
The slick has grown from about **45 sq km** in late July to roughly **800 sq km** by early August, and has now reached Oman's mainland coast.
It threatens the **Hallaniyat Islands** nature reserve, home to nesting sea turtles and the rare **Arabian Sea humpback whale**.
No country or group has claimed responsibility for the **explosion** that crippled the ship, and no party has yet accepted cleanup liability.
stories.background: Since Western sanctions hit Russian oil exports over the Ukraine war, a "shadow fleet" of aging, opaquely-owned tankers has grown up to keep that oil moving — dodging mainstream insurers and price-cap rules by operating outside normal maritime oversight. The **Caroline Bezengi**, a 274-metre tanker identified as part of that fleet, first reported an explosion onboard on **June 8** off Yemen and has been slowly sinking ever since near **Al Qibliyah Island** in Oman's **Hallaniyat Islands** — a protected marine reserve. Because shadow-fleet ships are deliberately hard to trace to a responsible owner or insurer, incidents like this one are difficult to hold anyone accountable for.
stories.what_happened: Oman's Environment Authority confirmed this week that oil leaking from the grounded, partly-submerged Caroline Bezengi has now reached the country's mainland beaches, around **Ras Madrakah**, some 200 km north of the islands where the tanker first ran into trouble. The slick has expanded dramatically — from roughly **45 square kilometers** on July 26 to about **800 square kilometers** by August 7, according to satellite tracking cited by the Associated Press — with up to **40 km of coastline** now affected. The tanker was carrying close to **one million barrels** of Russian crude when the explosion happened in June, and monsoon-season winds and currents have been pushing the spill further and faster than initially expected.
stories.why_it_matters: This is unfolding inside a protected marine reserve that supports coral reefs, seagrass beds, nesting sea turtles and one of the world's rarest whale populations — and it illustrates a real-world cost of sanctions evasion: shadow-fleet ships are often old, poorly maintained and effectively uninsured against exactly this kind of disaster.
stories.ripple_effects: Local fishing and tourism economies along Oman's coast face direct harm if the contamination keeps spreading. Because the tanker's true ownership and insurance are deliberately obscured, Oman may struggle to recover cleanup costs from anyone, which could sharpen international pressure for tighter rules on how shadow-fleet vessels are tracked, insured and inspected.
stories.why_now: The tanker has been slowly sinking and leaking since June, but the spill only reached Oman's populated mainland coastline in the past few days, turning a slow-building disaster into breaking news.
stories.watch_next: Whether Oman can contain or cap the remaining leak before more of the tanker's cargo escapes, and whether any government, insurer, or shipping entity accepts responsibility for the cleanup.

key_terms.definition: A network of aging, often unregistered or opaquely-owned tankers used to move sanctioned oil — commonly Russian — while evading Western insurance rules and price caps.
Financial or trade restrictions one country imposes on another to pressure a policy change; ships built to dodge them are often old and poorly maintained, raising accident risk.

stories.the_lesson: Sanctions evasion has real physical-world costs — vessels built to dodge insurance and registry rules are often cutting corners in maintenance too, so moving sanctioned cargo this way raises the odds of accidents like this one, with nobody clearly on the hook to pay for the damage.
stories.market_link: Adds to a summer of disruption around sanctioned Russian oil flows and Gulf-region shipping risk, though this spill itself is not near a major crude chokepoint like the Strait of Hormuz.

stories.title: Trump's press secretary Karoline Leavitt is resigning at the end of August, to become a top campaign advisor
key_points: Karoline Leavitt, at **28** the youngest White House press secretary in history, is stepping down by **end of August**.
Trump says she'll become one of his **"top outside advisors"** ahead of the **November midterms**.
She had only recently returned from **parental leave** after the birth of her second child in May.
The prior record for youngest press secretary belonged to Ronald Ziegler, who was **29** under Nixon in 1969.
No successor has been named; reported contenders include **Katie Miller** and Fox host **Kari Lake**.
stories.background: The White House press secretary is the administration's daily public voice — the person who stands at the podium and takes reporters' questions on the record, shaping how the government's actions get explained to the public. Leavitt became the youngest person ever to hold the job when Trump named her to it in **November 2024**, ahead of his second term. She has been a close, combative defender of the administration's messaging since, making her departure notable well beyond a routine staff change.
stories.what_happened: President Trump announced on **Wednesday, August 12** that Karoline Leavitt will leave her post as White House press secretary by the end of the month. Leavitt, 28, had returned to the podium only weeks earlier after parental leave for the birth of her second child in **May**. Trump said she is leaving **"so she can spend more time with her beautiful young children and family, a decision I totally understand and respect,"** and that she will instead become **one of his top outside advisors**, working with the Republican Party to help win the **November midterm elections**. Trump did not name a successor. Reporting has floated **Katie Miller** (wife of aide Stephen Miller, herself a former administration communications official) and Fox News host **Kari Lake** as possible replacements, though nothing is confirmed.
stories.why_it_matters: The press secretary is the administration's front line with the press and, through it, the public — a change in that role changes how the White House communicates heading into a contested midterm stretch. It also fits a broader pattern of officials in this administration rotating from formal government roles into campaign-facing "advisor" positions.
stories.ripple_effects: A new press secretary will need to rebuild rapport with the White House press corps from scratch during a politically charged run-up to the midterms. Leavitt's shift into a campaign-advisory role blurs — legally, but visibly — the line between government communications and party politics, a pattern likely to draw scrutiny from watchdogs and opposition Democrats alike.
stories.why_now: The announcement comes just weeks after Leavitt returned from parental leave, and with the November midterms close enough that Trump is reshuffling messaging roles to prioritize campaign support.
stories.watch_next: Who Trump names as the next White House press secretary before Leavitt's exit at the end of August.

key_terms.definition: The official who briefs journalists daily on behalf of the president and serves as the administration's primary public spokesperson.

stories.the_lesson: Administrations often route departing officials into "advisor" roles rather than a clean exit — it keeps loyalists close to the operation while blurring the formal line between government communications and campaign politics.

stories.title: Iran says the Strait of Hormuz is still shut despite Trump's claims, as tanker traffic sinks to a one-week low
key_points: Iran's Persian Gulf Strait Authority insists the **Strait of Hormuz remains blocked**, contradicting repeated US claims that it has reopened.
Tracked vessel transits fell to just **8 ships a day** — the lowest since August 5 — versus roughly **130 a day** before the war started in late February.
Iran has laid out conditions to fully reopen the strait: the **US must withdraw military assets, lift sanctions, and compensate Iran** for war and environmental damage.
The **International Energy Agency** is warning that global oil stockpiles are being drawn down fast as the standoff drags on.
stories.background: The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow waterway between Iran and Oman that roughly **one-fifth of the world's oil and gas** normally passes through by tanker — making it one of the most important chokepoints in the global economy. Fighting between the US and Iran broke out in late February, and Iran has kept the strait effectively closed ever since, despite President Trump repeatedly insisting the US has 'total control' over it and that it's open.
stories.what_happened: President Trump again insisted this week that the US has total control over the Strait of Hormuz and might 'keep it.' Iran's Persian Gulf Strait Authority directly contradicted that, saying the waterway remains blocked. Shipping trackers show the number of vessels transiting the strait fell to a one-week low of about **8 ships a day**, well below the recent 10-day average of around 12, and a fraction of the roughly 130 ships a day that used it before the war. Iran's Supreme National Security Council issued a list of demands before it will fully reopen the strait: the US must never threaten Iran again, end the blockade, withdraw all military assets from the region, lift sanctions, unfreeze Iranian assets, and pay compensation for war damage. Iran's foreign ministry also wants compensation specifically for pollution caused by the conflict in Gulf waters. The IEA has separately warned that global oil stockpiles are being burned through at a rapid pace as the standoff continues.
stories.why_it_matters: This is a direct threat to global energy supply — every day the strait stays effectively closed, oil that would normally flow to markets doesn't, which keeps upward pressure on fuel prices worldwide and adds to inflation risk everywhere, including in oil-importing countries like India.
stories.ripple_effects: Continued low tanker traffic keeps crude oil prices elevated, raises shipping and insurance costs on alternate routes, and squeezes countries most dependent on Gulf oil imports. It also raises the odds that dwindling global oil stockpiles turn a regional standoff into a broader price shock.
stories.why_now: The IEA's fresh warning about fast-depleting oil stockpiles raises the stakes just as Iran hardens its public list of conditions, making a near-term resolution look less likely.
stories.watch_next: Whether tanker traffic through the strait recovers or falls further, and whether the US and Iran resume direct talks given the IEA's stockpile warning.

key_terms.definition: A narrow sea passage between Iran and Oman that a large share of the world's traded oil and gas must pass through — one of the most important chokepoints in global energy trade.
Reserves of crude oil and refined fuel held by governments and companies as a buffer against supply disruptions; when they're drawn down quickly, prices become more sensitive to further shocks.

stories.the_lesson: Global energy chokepoints give small countries outsized leverage over the world economy — a strait a few dozen kilometers wide can move oil prices everywhere, war or no war.
stories.market_link: Crude benchmarks and energy-linked stocks stay in focus as the standoff drags on; India, a major oil importer, faces continued pressure on the rupee and its oil import bill the longer this lasts.

stories.title: China and Indonesia hold their first-ever joint navy drill east of Taiwan, and Taipei calls it a 'military provocation'
key_points: A **Chinese warship and an Indonesian frigate** are running a joint 'passage exercise' in waters **east of Taiwan** — the first time China has drilled with a foreign navy there.
Taiwan's China-policy body condemned it as **'CCP military provocation'**, saying it falsely implies China has jurisdiction over those waters.
Indonesia's navy says the drill is **routine**, calling it a standard 'passing exercise' on the way home from a port visit to **Russia**.
It's part of a broader pattern of China projecting military reach near Taiwan using **third-country partners**, not just its own fleet.
stories.background: Beijing claims Taiwan as its own territory and has spent years ramping up military pressure around the island — near-daily jet incursions, large-scale drills, and coast guard patrols meant to normalize a Chinese presence in disputed waters. Taiwan, a self-governing democracy of 23 million people, rejects that claim and is informally backed by the **United States**, which sells it weapons and has long signaled it would help defend the island if attacked. Indonesia is not a China ally in any formal sense — it's the world's largest Muslim-majority nation and usually prizes non-alignment — which is what makes this joint drill notable.
stories.what_happened: China's defence ministry said a Chinese warship and an Indonesian frigate conducted a 'passage exercise' in waters east of Taiwan in mid-August, describing it as meant to 'enhance the joint operational capabilities of the two navies' and 'jointly safeguard regional peace and stability.' It is the first time China has held a naval drill with a foreign military specifically in those waters. Taiwan's Mainland Affairs Council strongly condemned the move, accusing Beijing of trying to create the false impression that China has jurisdiction over waters east of Taiwan and calling it a violation of Taiwan's sovereignty. Indonesia's navy pushed back on the framing, saying the exercise is a routine 'passing exercise' — a 'universal naval tradition' conducted while transiting another country's maritime area — as the Indonesian ship returned from a visit to Russia. Taipei Times reported the story as still developing as of August 13.
stories.why_it_matters: Every time China normalizes a new kind of military activity near Taiwan — this time by bringing in a foreign partner — it makes the next escalation look a little more routine. It also puts Indonesia, a country that prizes its non-aligned status, in an uncomfortable spot: seen as lending legitimacy to Chinese military activity Taiwan considers a sovereignty violation.
stories.ripple_effects: Watch for Washington and Tokyo, both of which back Taiwan's de facto autonomy, to push back diplomatically. It could also complicate Indonesia's relationships with Taiwan and with Western partners wary of Chinese military partnerships in the Indo-Pacific, and adds another data point to how markets price 'Taiwan Strait risk' — a factor that matters hugely for chipmakers like TSMC given the island's central role in global semiconductor supply.
stories.why_now: It follows months of intensifying Chinese pressure on Taiwan and comes as China has been actively courting military-cooperation partners across Asia — using a 'routine' label to make expansion of its presence harder to formally object to.
stories.watch_next: Whether Indonesia agrees to further joint drills with China near Taiwan, and how the US and Japan respond diplomatically in the coming days.

key_terms.definition: A relatively low-key naval drill conducted while a ship transits through or near another country's waters, often used to signal presence without a full military exercise.
Beijing's position that Taiwan is part of China, not a separate country — a claim Taiwan's government rejects.

stories.the_lesson: Sovereignty over contested waters is enforced as much through symbolism and repetition as through law — a 'routine' drill repeated enough times can quietly shift what the world treats as normal.
stories.market_link: Escalating China-Taiwan tension is a standing risk factor for chipmakers like TSMC and Taiwan-exposed supply chains, though this specific drill has not moved markets so far.

stories.title: Colombia's 72-hour rescue window closes as the toll passes 220 and aid refusals spark backlash

thread.previously: We reported the confirmed death toll had risen to at least 224, with 700 injured and roughly 5,000 homes damaged or destroyed; Colombia's newly inaugurated president gave the first full damage briefing, and a woman was pulled alive from rubble after 30 hours.
thread.changed: The critical **72-hour survival window** — the point after which the odds of finding people alive in collapsed buildings drop sharply — has now effectively closed. It has also emerged that Colombia's government initially turned away most foreign rescue offers, asking for help from only four countries (the US, El Salvador, Ecuador and Israel) and citing sole reliance on domestic rescuers — a decision now drawing criticism as the young government's first real crisis controversy.

key_points: The critical **72-hour survival window** for finding people alive in rubble has effectively closed, four days after the quake.
Colombia initially **limited foreign rescue offers to just four countries**, relying mainly on domestic teams — a choice now under public criticism.
Forensic authorities put the death toll at **over 227**, higher than the government's own count, with the true figure still likely rising.
**Peru** has now confirmed it will send volunteers, after Colombia widened its request for outside help.
This is being called the **first major controversy** of new president Abelardo de la Espriella's government.
stories.background: A **magnitude-7.4 earthquake** struck western Colombia's coffee-growing region on Sunday, August 9, and is the country's deadliest in decades. It leveled buildings across Chocó and hit hardest in Cali, Pereira, Manizales and Quibdó, with roads into the epicenter near San José del Palmar blocked by landslides for days. The disaster landed just days into the term of Colombia's new hard-right president, Abelardo de la Espriella, making it the first major crisis test of his administration.
stories.what_happened: As the **72-hour survival window** narrowed and then closed, Colombia's government confirmed it had initially declined most international rescue offers, requesting help from only the **US, El Salvador, Ecuador and Israel** and stating it would rely on national rescuers instead — a marked contrast to how neighboring Venezuela accepted dozens of foreign teams without question after its own recent quakes. Colombian forensic authorities separately put the death toll at **more than 227**, above the government's own running count, while roughly **195 people remain officially listed as missing** — though volunteer-run databases estimate the real number closer to **4,000**, reflecting how hard it is to get an accurate count with damaged phone networks and blocked roads. Peru has now confirmed it will dispatch volunteers to help. Colombia's disaster-management chief defended the limited outside help, denying any ideological motive behind the decision.
stories.why_it_matters: The closing of the 72-hour window means rescue operations are now shifting from a race to save survivors toward recovery — while the decision to limit foreign help, made in the most critical early hours, will likely be scrutinized as a factor in how many people could still be saved.
stories.ripple_effects: The political backlash over the aid decision adds pressure on a brand-new government already managing a mass-casualty disaster, and could shape how quickly Colombia accepts international help in future emergencies. The economic cost — from destroyed homes to disrupted local businesses — will weigh on Chocó and Valle del Cauca's regional economies for months.
stories.why_now: Four days have now passed since the quake struck on August 9, pushing the disaster past the point where survival odds for anyone still trapped drop sharply — making today the natural moment the rescue-to-recovery shift becomes official.
stories.watch_next: Watch for Colombia's next official casualty update and whether the government formally opens the door to a wider range of international rescue and reconstruction assistance.
stories.the_lesson: In the first hours after a disaster, a government's choices about accepting outside help can matter as much as the disaster itself — pride or politics in a crisis window can cost lives that logistics alone wouldn't have.

stories.title: Ukraine hits Russia's last safe Black Sea Fleet harbor at Novorossiysk, damaging four warships
key_points: **Four Russian warships** were damaged — two frigates (Admiral Makarov, Admiral Essen), a missile ship (Buyan-M), and a patrol ship (Vasily Bykov).
Novorossiysk sits more than **300 kilometers** from the front line and had become Russia's main safe harbor after Crimea's ports were made too dangerous.
Ukraine combined **Palianytsia jet-powered drones**, Neptune cruise missiles, and naval drones in the strike — a mix it couldn't field a few years ago.
The attack also hit the **Sheskharis oil terminal**, one of Russia's largest crude-export points, and an S-300 air-defense radar guarding the base.
President Zelensky called it a **'unique operation'** targeting what was left of Russia's Black Sea safe harbor.
stories.background: Novorossiysk, on Russia's Black Sea coast, became the main home of the **Black Sea Fleet** after two years of Ukrainian missile and drone strikes made Crimean ports like Sevastopol too dangerous to anchor in. The port does double duty as one of Russia's biggest oil-export terminals, moving crude that arrives via pipeline from deep inland. Through 2026, Ukraine has steadily extended the range and reliability of its domestically built long-range drones and missiles, pushing further from the front line than it could a year or two ago. This strike is the latest sign that no Russian Black Sea harbor is now truly out of reach.
stories.what_happened: Overnight on **August 12**, Ukraine's military carried out what President Zelensky called a 'unique operation' against the naval base at Novorossiysk, more than **300 kilometers** from the nearest front line. Ukrainian forces combined **Palianytsia jet-powered attack drones**, Neptune anti-ship cruise missiles, and uncrewed naval drones in the strike. Four Russian warships were damaged: the frigates **Admiral Makarov** and **Admiral Essen**, the missile ship **Buyan-M**, and the patrol ship **Vasily Bykov**. The strike also hit an S-300 air-defense radar protecting the port and the **Sheskharis oil terminal**, a major crude-export point, along with infrastructure across several piers. Russian officials have not published a detailed damage assessment.
stories.why_it_matters: Novorossiysk was supposed to be the safe harbor Russia's navy retreated to once Crimea's ports became too dangerous — this strike shows even that refuge is now within Ukraine's reach. It also puts a major Russian oil-export route directly in the line of fire, which matters for global crude supply.
stories.ripple_effects: Russia's Black Sea Fleet has now lost most of its historically safe anchorages, which may push it to disperse ships further east or accept that it can no longer operate safely in the western Black Sea at all. Any lasting damage to the Sheskharis terminal could disrupt Russian crude exports — a second front-line risk for oil traders already watching the separate Strait of Hormuz standoff between the US and Iran.
stories.why_now: Ukraine has spent 2026 scaling up production of longer-range drones and missiles, and Novorossiysk — long considered safely out of range — is the latest target to fall inside that expanding envelope.
stories.watch_next: Watch for satellite imagery confirming how badly the four warships and the oil terminal were damaged, and whether Russia starts relocating remaining Black Sea Fleet assets further from the coast.

key_terms.definition: The branch of Russia's navy based in the Black Sea, historically headquartered in Crimea before Ukrainian strikes forced much of it to relocate.
A Ukrainian-made jet-powered strike drone that functions like a low-cost cruise missile, used to hit targets deep inside Russia.

stories.the_lesson: Long-range drones let a militarily smaller country keep extending real strike pressure hundreds of kilometers past the front line — in a drone war, distance from the fighting no longer guarantees safety the way it used to.
stories.market_link: Any confirmed lasting damage to the Sheskharis oil terminal could tighten Russian crude exports, adding a second source of upward pressure on Brent prices alongside the separate Strait of Hormuz standoff.

stories.title: An overloaded ferry capsizes on Zimbabwe's Lake Kariba, killing at least 44
key_points: At least **44 people have drowned** after a passenger ferry capsized on Lake Kariba, with dozens still missing.
The boat's official capacity was **90 people** — it was carrying **114 adult passengers**, 5 crew, and an unspecified number of children.
A survivor says passengers **begged the driver to turn back** because of choppy water, but he refused.
Lake Kariba is the **world's largest man-made lake** and a vital transport link for islands and fishing villages with no roads.
A specialized aquatic rescue unit was **airlifted in** to search for survivors and recover bodies.
stories.background: Lake Kariba, formed by a dam on the Zambezi River, is the largest artificial lake in the world by volume, and it sits between Zimbabwe and Zambia. Because many communities on its shores and islands have no road access, government-run ferries are often the only practical way for people to travel, trade, and reach markets or hospitals. That reliance on a handful of aging vessels is exactly why overcrowding is a chronic risk on routes like this one.
stories.what_happened: A government passenger ferry that runs between the town of Kariba and surrounding islands and fishing villages capsized in choppy conditions, killing at least **44 people** so far, with search and rescue operations still ongoing for dozens more who remain missing. The vessel's rated capacity was 90 people, but it was carrying at least **114 adult passengers** plus 5 crew members and an unknown number of children when it went down — meaning it was significantly overloaded. A survivor told Zimbabwe's national broadcaster, ZBC, that passengers had pleaded with the ferry operator to turn back once the water got rough, but he refused to do so. Authorities have deployed a specialized aquatic rescue unit by air to the area, and two funeral parlors have been engaged to handle recovery of the dead.
stories.why_it_matters: This is one of the deadliest transport disasters in the region in years, and it exposes a familiar and preventable pattern: overcrowded, under-regulated ferries carrying people who have no safer alternative. The driver's refusal to turn back despite passenger warnings points to a systemic safety and accountability gap, not just bad weather.
stories.ripple_effects: Expect scrutiny of Zimbabwe's ferry licensing and capacity-enforcement rules, and possibly similar reviews across other Southern African countries that rely on lake and river ferries. Families in the fishing and farming communities served by this route face an immediate loss of a critical transport link on top of the human tragedy.
stories.why_now: The capsizing happened this week as the ferry was making a routine crossing in rough water, and the death toll is still rising as search teams recover more bodies and locate survivors.
stories.watch_next: Whether Zimbabwean authorities open a formal investigation into the ferry's overcrowding and the operator's decision-making, and whether the final death toll rises further.
stories.the_lesson: Overcrowding on transport that serves communities with no alternative route is a recurring cause of mass-casualty accidents worldwide — the danger isn't usually the weather alone, it's a vessel carrying far more people than it was built to carry.

stories.title: Colombia's earthquake toll climbs as rescuers race the 72-hour survival window

thread.previously: We reported the magnitude-7.4 quake that hit Colombia's Chocó department had killed more than 220 people, with President Abelardo de la Espriella saying at least 5,000 homes were destroyed.
thread.changed: Colombian authorities now confirm at least 181 dead and 2,595 injured as the official count is re-verified, with 195 more listed as missing officially — though civilian-run databases put that figure closer to 4,000. Search teams are racing against the 72-hour mark after which survival chances in collapsed buildings drop sharply, and rescuers still can't reach the epicenter near San José del Palmar.

key_points: Colombian officials confirm **at least 181 dead** and **2,595 injured** as of Wednesday's count, two days after the quake.
**195 people are officially missing**, but volunteer-run databases put the real number closer to **4,000**.
Rescue teams are racing the **72-hour survival window** — the point after which chances of finding survivors in rubble fall steeply.
Roads into the epicenter near **San José del Palmar** remain blocked, so some of the worst-hit areas still haven't been reached.
The disaster is the first major crisis test for Colombia's new president, **Abelardo de la Espriella**.
stories.background: A magnitude-7.4 earthquake struck Colombia's mountainous Chocó department on Monday, August 10, one of the strongest quakes to hit the country in decades. The region is remote and poorly connected, which is why it has taken days for rescue teams and even accurate casualty counts to reach the outside world. Colombia's government changed hands earlier this year, and this is the **first major natural disaster** the new administration has had to manage.
stories.what_happened: The quake leveled homes across Chocó, and the official death toll — verified case by case by Colombian authorities — stands at **181**, with **2,595 people injured**. Officials list **195 more as missing**, but volunteer networks tracking family reports separately estimate the true number of unaccounted-for people is closer to **4,000**, reflecting how hard it is to get an accurate count in a disaster zone with damaged phone networks and blocked roads. Search-and-rescue teams are now in a race against the **72-hour mark** since the quake struck — the rough threshold after which the odds of finding people alive in collapsed buildings drop off sharply. Rescuers still haven't been able to physically reach the epicenter near San José del Palmar because access roads are damaged or blocked by landslides.
stories.why_it_matters: This is shaping up as one of the deadliest natural disasters in Colombia in years, and it's testing a brand-new government's ability to respond to a crisis at scale. The gap between the official missing count (195) and the civilian estimate (near 4,000) shows how much uncertainty still surrounds the true scale of the disaster.
stories.ripple_effects: Colombia will likely need significant international aid and reconstruction financing, which could strain its budget and draw in agencies like the Red Cross and UN disaster relief bodies. The remoteness of Chocó — one of Colombia's poorest regions — means rebuilding will be slow and could deepen existing inequality between it and wealthier parts of the country.
stories.why_now: Search teams are hitting the critical 72-hour survival window this week, which is why casualty figures are being revised and rescue urgency is peaking right now.
stories.watch_next: Whether rescue teams can reach the blocked-off epicenter near San José del Palmar in the next day or two, and whether the missing count converges toward the official or the civilian estimate.

key_terms.definition: The rough time frame after a building collapse during which trapped survivors have meaningfully better odds of being found alive; rescue efforts intensify as this deadline approaches.

stories.the_lesson: In disasters that hit remote, poorly connected regions, the official casualty count and the on-the-ground reality can diverge sharply for days — damaged infrastructure doesn't just kill people, it also blinds the people trying to help them.

stories.title: Researchers find a flaw that let weaker AI models leak stronger models' hidden reasoning — and even passwords
key_points: Security researchers showed **OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google's** AI systems could be tricked into revealing their **encrypted internal "reasoning"** — normally hidden from users.
The trick: replaying a hidden-reasoning block from one session into **a weaker model** in the same family, which lacks the safety filtering to refuse and just prints it out.
Across **6,708 public AI-agent conversation logs**, researchers decoded **315,320 hidden reasoning blocks**, some containing **leaked API keys and passwords**.

The flaw enables **four types of abuse**: stealing reasoning to copy a rival's model, extracting private user data, uncovering content models were told to hide, and smuggling hidden instructions past safety checks.
stories.background: Modern AI "reasoning" models think through a problem in a hidden scratchpad before giving their final answer — a technique that improves accuracy but that companies keep encrypted and invisible to protect their trade secrets and prevent misuse. Developers who build tools on top of these models sometimes need to pass that hidden reasoning between separate API calls to keep a conversation coherent, which is where this flaw lived. A research team published a paper titled "Stealing Reasoning Traces from Proprietary LLM APIs" documenting how they exploited this.
stories.what_happened: The researchers found that an encrypted reasoning block created in one session could be **replayed into a different session** and, if handed to a **cheaper, lighter model from the same company**, would sometimes get decoded and printed out in plain text — because lighter models are built with less aggressive filtering than a company's flagship model. Testing this against thousands of publicly logged AI-agent conversations, the team recovered **over 315,000 hidden reasoning blocks**, some of which contained sensitive data like API keys and passwords that had leaked into a model's internal reasoning. The three companies have since updated how they handle this: **Anthropic** now says reasoning blocks are tied to the specific model that created them and should be discarded when switching models; **Google** says its backend manages compatibility automatically; **OpenAI** still instructs developers to replay reasoning blocks manually.
stories.why_it_matters: AI companies spend enormous sums building the "reasoning" ability into their models and treat how it works as a competitive secret — this flaw showed that secret wasn't as protected as assumed, and that ordinary developer conversation logs could contain leaked passwords without anyone realizing it.
stories.ripple_effects: Companies building on these AI APIs need to check whether their own logs of past conversations expose secrets, and AI vendors face pressure to close similar gaps as reasoning models become standard across the industry. It also renews scrutiny on how much AI companies can genuinely keep proprietary as rivals get better at extracting it.
stories.why_now: The vulnerability was published this week as researchers disclosed the paper and vendors began responding with documentation and behavior changes.
stories.watch_next: Whether OpenAI follows Anthropic and Google in changing how encrypted reasoning is handled across model switches, and whether any real-world leaked credentials are confirmed to have caused harm.

key_terms.definition: The hidden step-by-step "thinking" an AI model does internally before giving its final answer — normally not shown to the user.
Training a smaller, cheaper AI model to copy a larger one's behavior — something companies try to prevent rivals from doing to their proprietary models.

stories.the_lesson: Any system that must pass "private" internal data between separate calls or sessions creates a seam where that data can leak — encryption alone doesn't help if the receiving side can be tricked into decoding it for you.

stories.title: US-Iran talks on reopening the Strait of Hormuz break down, and oil prices rise on the deadlock
key_points: Oil prices climbed after **Iran added new demands** — including eased US sanctions and **war reparations** — before it will reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

The strait normally carries about **one-fifth of the world's oil supply**; shipping through it has collapsed to **8–15 vessels crossing on Aug 4–6**, versus roughly **130 transits before the conflict**.
Iran's Supreme Leader reshuffled the country's **top military leadership**, naming new armed forces and Revolutionary Guard commanders.
President Trump said the US has **"total control"** of the strait and warned Iran would **"get blown away"** if it interfered with shipping there.
stories.background: Since a US-Israel-Iran war erupted in late February 2026, Iranian attacks on shipping and US retaliatory strikes have repeatedly disrupted the **Strait of Hormuz**, the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman that oil tankers must pass through to leave the Gulf. Periodic ceasefire efforts and partial truces have not held, and Trump has followed a pattern of threatening major new strikes and then pulling back. Earlier in August, Iran appeared close to a deal with Oman on managing traffic through the strait, which briefly lifted hopes of it reopening.
stories.what_happened: Iran told mediators that a technical agreement with Oman on strait management **would not be enough on its own** — Tehran is now also demanding the US ease sanctions and pay war reparations before it will let normal shipping resume. Talks stalled as a result, and **oil prices rose** on the fading odds of a quick resolution: Brent crude settled near **$89 a barrel** and US crude (WTI) near **$83**. Iran's Supreme Leader Khamenei's son and de facto successor, Mojtaba Khamenei, named a new military high command, including Ali Abdollahi as armed forces chief of staff. Trump reiterated that the US would not tolerate interference with shipping, while Gulf states have grown visibly frustrated at being caught between the two sides.
stories.why_it_matters: Around a fifth of the world's traded oil normally passes through this one chokepoint, so a prolonged closure keeps a floor under global oil and fuel prices — raising costs for households and businesses far from the Middle East. It also shows how close a full ceasefire can look, then unravel, when each side keeps adding new conditions.
stories.ripple_effects: Higher and more volatile oil prices feed into inflation readings worldwide, complicating central banks' interest-rate decisions (including the US Federal Reserve's, due mid-September). Countries that import most of their oil, including India, face a bigger import bill and pressure on their currencies — India's rupee has already been sliding partly because of this same standoff.
stories.why_now: The breakdown follows days of cautious optimism after Iran signaled a deal with Oman was close; adding fresh demands on sanctions and reparations shows Tehran is using the leverage of continued disruption rather than settling quickly.
stories.watch_next: Whether Saudi Arabia's diplomatic push — Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has urged Trump to hold off on further strikes — produces a new round of talks before shipping losses deepen further.

key_terms.definition: A narrow sea passage between Iran and Oman that nearly all oil shipped out of the Gulf must sail through — a natural chokepoint for the global oil trade.
The two most widely quoted oil price benchmarks — Brent for oil traded internationally, WTI (West Texas Intermediate) for US oil.

stories.the_lesson: Chokepoints — narrow physical passages that a large share of global trade must funnel through — give small players outsized leverage over prices everyone pays, because disrupting the passage is far cheaper than the economic damage it causes downstream.
stories.market_link: Crude oil (Brent/WTI), airline and shipping stocks, and oil-import-dependent currencies like the Indian rupee are directly exposed to how long the strait stays disrupted.

thread.previously: Yesterday's coverage focused on the rupee and Indian oil companies bleeding money as the strait stayed shut, with a deal seen as unlikely soon.
thread.changed: Today the block is explicitly on the diplomatic track: Iran has added new demands (sanctions relief, reparations) that talks with Oman alone can't satisfy, oil prices have ticked up in response, and Iran has also reshuffled its military command.
