stories.title: India's Supreme Court grows from 34 to 38 judges as President Murmu signs off on the expansion
key_points: President **Droupadi Murmu** has assented to the **Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Act, 2026**, raising the court's sanctioned strength from **34 to 38 judges**, including the Chief Justice.
It's the **first increase since 2019**, when the number (excluding the CJI) rose from 30 to 33.
The government cites **over 92,000 pending cases** as of January 2026 — the court registered **75,410 new cases** in 2025 but disposed of only about **65,000**.
The law is treated as effective from **May 16, 2026**, the date the President first promulgated it as an ordinance, ahead of Parliament formally passing the Bill.
Parliament passed the Bill this month: **Lok Sabha on August 3**, and the **Rajya Sabha returned it on August 5**.
stories.background: India's Supreme Court is the country's final court of appeal and constitutional arbiter, and its sanctioned strength — the maximum number of judges allowed by law — has been raised only a handful of times as caseloads grew, most recently in 2019. More judges lets the court sit as more simultaneous benches, which matters because most of its work happens in small panels of two or three judges hearing thousands of appeals a year, alongside larger constitutional benches for major cases. The government first raised the judge count by **ordinance** — a temporary law the President can issue when Parliament isn't in session — before Parliament converted it into a permanent Act this month.
stories.what_happened: President **Droupadi Murmu** signed the **Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Act, 2026** into law, raising the court's sanctioned strength from **34 to 38 judges** (including the Chief Justice of India). Law minister **Arjun Ram Meghwal** introduced the Bill in the Lok Sabha on **July 20**; the Lok Sabha passed it on **August 3**, and the Rajya Sabha returned it on **August 5**, before it went to the President for assent on **August 11**. The Act is treated as effective from **May 16, 2026** — the date the President had already promulgated an ordinance version of the change, ahead of Parliament passing the full law. The government justified the expansion by pointing to **more than 92,000 cases pending** before the Supreme Court as of January 1, 2026, after the court took in 75,410 new cases in 2025 but disposed of only around 65,000. This is the first change to the court's sanctioned strength since 2019.
stories.why_it_matters: A bigger bench count lets the Supreme Court run more parallel hearings, the main lever available to cut a backlog that's grown for years and directly affects how long ordinary litigants — from property disputes to criminal appeals — wait for a final ruling.
stories.ripple_effects: The Chief Justice-led collegium — the small group of senior judges that recommends judicial appointments in India — must now identify and recommend four additional judges, likely shaping who sits on the top court for the next decade. Faster case turnover could also affect how quickly high-stakes commercial and constitutional disputes that matter to investors and businesses get resolved.
stories.why_now: The move follows a familiar pattern in India — an ordinance in May let the change take effect immediately, and Parliament's monsoon session in July-August gave lawmakers their first chance to convert it into permanent law.
stories.watch_next: Watch for the collegium's recommendations on who fills the four new seats — that process, historically, is where disputes between the judiciary and government over judicial independence tend to surface.

key_terms.definition: The maximum number of judges a court is legally allowed to have at one time — actual appointments can run below this ceiling.
A law the Indian President can issue when Parliament isn't in session, which must later be approved by Parliament to stay in force.

stories.the_lesson: Court backlogs are often a capacity problem as much as a legal one — adding judges is usually the most direct, if slow, lever governments have to speed up justice.

stories.title: Gold nears ₹1.55 lakh per 10 grams in India — a record fueled more by the falling rupee than global prices
key_points: MCX gold futures touched an intraday high of **₹1,54,950 per 10 grams** on Wednesday, within reach of the **₹1.55 lakh** mark — a fresh domestic record.
Silver jumped even harder, gaining **₹2,314** on the session to trade near **₹2,55,000 per kg**.

Global spot gold is actually **well below** its all-time high — it peaked at **$5,602/oz in January 2026** and now sits around **$4,495/oz** — so India's record is driven mainly by **rupee weakness**.
The rupee has been sliding as the **Strait of Hormuz standoff** pushes oil prices up, and a weaker rupee mechanically raises the rupee price of gold.
Even as prices hit records, India's jewellery **demand fell about 15% year-on-year** in Q2 2026, per World Gold Council data, as buyers shift to lighter pieces and EMIs.
stories.background: Gold had a historic run in 2026, peaking at **$5,602/oz in January** on central-bank buying and rate-cut bets, before pulling back over 20%. The current push higher in India is layered on top of that — the same Strait of Hormuz crisis rattling oil markets is also weakening the rupee, and because Indian gold prices are set in rupees, currency weakness alone can push them to records even without a global price spike. Gold has long been India's default store of household savings, central to weddings and festivals.
stories.what_happened: On **Wednesday, August 12**, MCX gold futures rose ₹1,182 to trade around **₹1,54,280 per 10 grams**, with an intraday high of **₹1,54,950** — just short of the ₹1.55 lakh mark and a fresh all-time high in rupee terms. 24-karat gold worked out to roughly **₹15,486 per gram**. Silver moved even more sharply, up ₹2,314 on the day to near **₹2,55,000 per kg**. Internationally, spot gold held around **$4,495/oz** — well below its January 2026 peak of $5,602 — meaning the Indian record reflects rupee depreciation more than fresh global demand. Traders were also watching crude oil, which held near $89/barrel (WTI), and awaiting US inflation data for clues on the Federal Reserve's next rate move.
stories.why_it_matters: Gold is the most common way ordinary Indian households store savings, so a record price is a direct, felt cost — especially heading into the autumn wedding season and Raksha Bandhan on **August 28**. It's also a clean way to see currency depreciation show up in everyday prices.
stories.ripple_effects: Record gold prices raise India's import bill for the metal, adding to a current-account deficit already stretched by the Strait of Hormuz standoff's effect on oil costs; the trade deficit had already widened to **$37.4 billion** in the first quarter of the fiscal year. Jewellers may see revenue hold up even as volumes fall, as buyers shift toward EMIs and gold-savings schemes.
stories.why_now: The move is a direct pass-through of the rupee's slide this week, itself driven by the ongoing Strait of Hormuz standoff pushing oil prices higher.
stories.watch_next: Whether the rupee stabilizes if a Hormuz shipping deal materializes (which would likely cap gold's rupee price), and upcoming US inflation data for Fed rate-cut signals that move gold globally.

key_terms.definition: The gap between what a country pays for imports (like oil and gold) and what it earns from exports and other foreign income — a wider gap usually weakens the currency over time.

stories.the_lesson: A 'record price' in your local currency doesn't always mean a global record — currency depreciation alone can push a domestically-priced asset to new highs even while the underlying global price is falling.
stories.market_link: Gold and silver futures (MCX), rupee-sensitive importers and jewellery stocks are the direct plays; a weaker rupee also raises costs for oil-linked and import-heavy Indian companies.

stories.title: 'Lungiwala' remark sparks a privilege motion in the Rajya Sabha as BJP MP denies the charge
key_points: CPI(M) MP **John Brittas** filed a privilege motion against BJP MP **Sushmita Dev**, accusing her of repeatedly calling him "lungiwala" while he moved a resolution in the **Rajya Sabha on August 10**.
Brittas said he was wearing a **dhoti**, not a lungi, and called the remark a **"deliberate... derogatory stereotype"** about South Indians.
The House was disrupted and briefly **adjourned**; Chairman C.P. Radhakrishnan summoned both MPs to his chamber to resolve the dispute.
Leader of the House **J.P. Nadda** distanced the BJP from the remark, saying "we do not call it lungi; we call it dhoti," while asking that Dev also be heard.
Today, Dev **denied making the remark**, saying "no message from the House should divide India" — without apologizing.
stories.background: The incident happened during a debate on the Taxation and Other Laws (Amendment) Bill in the Rajya Sabha, as Brittas moved a resolution against a tax ordinance. It taps into a recurring fault line in Indian politics — allegations that Hindi-heartland politicians stereotype South Indian culture — which has flared before over language and revenue-sharing disputes. It's playing out during an already tense **Monsoon Session** dominated by protests, floods, and market shocks.
stories.what_happened: On **August 10, 2026**, while CPI(M) Rajya Sabha MP John Brittas was speaking, BJP MP Sushmita Dev allegedly left her seat, sat behind him, and repeatedly called him "lungiwala" — a jibe referencing the lungi, a garment stereotypically associated with South Indians. Brittas, who said he was actually wearing a dhoti, filed a formal **privilege motion**, asking that the matter go to the Committee of Privileges for undermining the dignity of the House. The disruption forced Rajya Sabha Chairman C.P. Radhakrishnan to summon both MPs to his chamber, and the House was adjourned until 2 pm. Leader of the House J.P. Nadda told the chamber the BJP does not endorse such remarks but said Dev should get a chance to respond. Today, **August 12**, Dev denied the allegation on record, saying no message from Parliament should divide the country culturally, while stopping short of an apology.
stories.why_it_matters: If the Chairman refers the case to the Committee of Privileges, it could produce a formal reprimand of a sitting BJP MP — a genuinely unusual outcome in Indian parliamentary practice. It also hands opposition parties from South India a fresh talking point about disrespect from the Hindi-speaking political mainstream.
stories.ripple_effects: Expect Kerala and Tamil Nadu politicians to amplify the episode regionally, especially heading into the Independence Day period, and for it to resurface in future debates over delimitation and revenue-sharing between states.
stories.why_now: Dev's on-the-record denial came today, escalating what started as a floor disruption two days ago into an active dispute with a live privilege motion pending.
stories.watch_next: Whether the Rajya Sabha Chairman formally refers the matter to the Committee of Privileges, and whether Dev is asked to clarify or apologize on the floor.

key_terms.definition: A formal complaint an MP can file when they believe their dignity or the House's dignity has been breached — it can lead to a committee inquiry and, rarely, a reprimand.
India's upper house of Parliament, whose members are elected by state legislatures rather than directly by voters.

stories.the_lesson: Small floor-level disputes in Parliament can escalate into formal proceedings and regional political flashpoints when they touch identity or regional pride — process becomes the vehicle for a much bigger cultural argument.

stories.title: Monsoon turns deadly in central India as IMD widens its rain alert to 19 states
key_points: The **India Meteorological Department (IMD)** issued fresh heavy-rain and thunderstorm warnings for **19 states** today, including Delhi-NCR, Uttar Pradesh, Punjab and Rajasthan, with gusts up to **90 km/h**.

In Madhya Pradesh's **Rajgarh district**, a van carrying 11 people was swept into a flooded drain on Monday; **9 people, including 3 children, died**, and a search continues for the last missing passenger.
**Bhopal** recorded 74.5mm of rain in three hours, flooding more than **1,000 homes** and forcing rescuers to save 98 people and several animals.
Rajasthan's Jhalawar district received about **300mm (roughly 12 inches)** of rain, the state's heaviest this season, triggering an orange alert in six districts and shutting schools.
Madhya Pradesh Chief Minister **Mohan Yadav** announced ₹4 lakh in compensation for each family that lost a member in the Rajgarh tragedy.
stories.background: India's four-month monsoon season (June–September) delivers roughly 70% of the country's annual rainfall and is essential for farming, but it also triggers floods, landslides and flash floods almost every year — and this year has already been especially deadly, with **Himachal Pradesh** alone recording 157 deaths from floods and landslides. This week the crisis has widened into central India, with **Madhya Pradesh** and **Rajasthan** bearing the brunt of intense, localised downpours.
stories.what_happened: On Monday, a van carrying 11 people — three men, four women and four children — drove onto a flooded, under-construction bridge over the Jhiri drain near Padana village in Rajgarh despite warnings from locals and officials not to cross; the current swept the vehicle away and it sank within moments, killing 9 of the occupants, with a search continuing for the last person. The next day, Bhopal was hit by 74.5mm of rain in just three hours, flooding over 1,000 homes and forcing State Disaster Response Force teams and Home Guards to rescue 98 people and a number of stranded animals. Rajasthan's Jhalawar district recorded the state's heaviest rainfall of the season, around 300mm, swelling the Kalisindh and Ahu rivers enough to cut off roughly 10 villages and strand pilgrims near a riverside temple. Today the IMD extended its alert further, warning of heavy to very heavy rain and storms across 19 states, from Jammu & Kashmir and Uttarakhand — where all 12 districts are under a flash-flood warning — down toward the south.
stories.why_it_matters: This isn't an isolated cloudburst — it's a widening, multi-state monsoon emergency that has already killed people in Madhya Pradesh and displaced families in Bhopal and Rajasthan, on top of the 157 deaths already recorded in Himachal Pradesh this season. When alerts span 19 states at once, it strains disaster-response resources nationally, not just in one region.
stories.ripple_effects: Flooded farmland and washed-out roads can dent crop yields and disrupt supply chains in India's agricultural heartland, and repeated disaster payouts add pressure to state budgets already stretched by relief spending. Recurring, erratic monsoon extremes also feed into the wider debate over how climate change is reshaping India's most important weather system.
stories.why_now: The IMD widened its alert to 19 states today as an active weather system continues pumping moisture across north and central India, even as the aftermath of Monday's and Tuesday's downpours is still being cleared up.
stories.watch_next: Watch the IMD's next 24-hour bulletin for whether the alert list grows or shrinks, and whether the search for the 11th Rajgarh victim concludes.

key_terms.definition: the India Meteorological Department, the government agency that forecasts weather and issues rain, storm and flood alerts.
IMD's colour-coded warning system — orange means 'be prepared' for very heavy weather, yellow means 'stay updated', red means 'take action' for extreme, dangerous weather.
a sudden, fast-rising flood, often within hours of intense rain, that gives little time to evacuate.

stories.the_lesson: Flood warnings exist because water can turn a normal-looking road or bridge lethal within seconds — the Rajgarh tragedy shows that ignoring a local warning about a submerged crossing, even briefly, can be the difference between a story and a headline.
stories.market_link: Crop damage across Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan, two significant agricultural states, could weigh on India's kharif (monsoon-sown) harvest outlook and add upside risk to food inflation later this year, though it is too early to size the impact.

stories.title: Lok Sabha sends contested FCRA bill, which lets the government seize NGOs' foreign-funded assets, to a joint panel
key_points: The Lok Sabha today passed a motion referring the **Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026** to a Joint Parliamentary Committee (JPC) for detailed review instead of a straight vote.
The JPC will have **31 members** — 21 from the Lok Sabha, 10 from the Rajya Sabha — and must report back by the first week of the **Winter Session**.
The bill creates a new **'Designated Authority'** that can take over and sell the assets of NGOs whose foreign-funding licence is cancelled, surrendered, or not renewed.
Congress's **Shashi Tharoor** and other opposition leaders say the bill hands government sweeping power over civil society; the **Kerala Assembly** has passed a resolution demanding it be withdrawn.
Proceeds from any sale of seized assets would go straight into the **Consolidated Fund of India**, the government's main account.
stories.background: The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, or **FCRA**, has governed how Indian NGOs, charities, and religious and educational institutions receive money from abroad since **2010**, requiring every recipient to register and report the funds. Union Minister of State for Home Affairs **Nityanand Rai** introduced this amendment bill in the Lok Sabha back in **March 2026** on behalf of Home Minister Amit Shah, and it has drawn sustained pushback since — from churches and missionary groups to international rights bodies — over how much control it gives the state.
stories.what_happened: On Wednesday, the government moved a motion to send the bill to a joint committee of both Houses rather than push it through for a final vote, after weeks of protest from the Opposition and civil society groups. The motion passed amid an Opposition uproar, with Congress, the Samajwadi Party and others demanding the bill be scrapped entirely rather than merely reviewed. The 31-member committee must submit its report by the last day of the first week of Parliament's Winter Session. At the bill's core is the new Designated Authority, which can take **provisional and then permanent control** of the money and property of any organisation that loses its FCRA registration, and then sell those assets — though it is barred from altering the religious character of a place of worship bought with foreign funds. The government says the changes close loopholes and tighten oversight of overseas money entering India; critics, including some foreign observers per earlier reporting, call it a tool to squeeze NGOs, churches and rights groups the state dislikes.
stories.why_it_matters: This is a fight over how much room India's civil society — NGOs, churches, human-rights groups, charities — gets to operate independent of government control, and over the fate of large sums of foreign funding that flow into health, education and rights work every year. Sending the bill to a JPC delays it but doesn't kill it, so the argument over its final shape continues.
stories.ripple_effects: Thousands of India-registered NGOs and international donors are watching closely, since the bill could decide whether their bank accounts and property survive if their FCRA licence lapses. It also touches India's external relationships at a sensitive moment — coverage has noted separate concern raised abroad about the bill — even as New Delhi is already managing friction with the US over tariffs and with China over the border.
stories.why_now: The referral happened today as Parliament's Monsoon Session nears its close, with the government opting to send the bill for further scrutiny after weeks of pressure rather than force it through.
stories.watch_next: Watch for the Joint Parliamentary Committee's member list and its report, due by the first week of the Winter Session.

key_terms.definition: the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, India's 2010 law controlling how NGOs and individuals receive money from outside the country.
a temporary panel of MPs from both houses of Parliament set up to study a bill or issue in detail before it returns for a final vote.
a new government-appointed body the bill creates to take over, and if needed sell, the assets of NGOs that lose their foreign-funding registration.
the government's main bank account, into which nearly all its revenues and receipts are deposited.

stories.the_lesson: When a government changes how money moves through civil society, watch not just the vote count but who gets custody of the assets if an organisation loses its licence — that detail usually reveals the law's real intent.

stories.title: Scotland and Canada clash again in Dundee with 2027 World Cup qualification hopes on the line
key_points: Scotland and Canada are playing their second meeting in a week in the **ICC Men's Cricket World Cup League 2**, this time in Dundee
Scotland sit **2nd** in the League 2 table with 38 points from 32 matches; Canada are **5th** with 20 points from 20 games
The two teams last met on **August 7**, when Scotland won by 9 runs in a high-scoring game (281/7 vs 272)
League 2 results feed directly into qualification for the **2027 Cricket World Cup** — making every match here count for both sides
Scotland reached **267/4** in their innings today, with Michael Jones unbeaten on 41, as they push to extend their points lead
stories.background: The **ICC Men's Cricket World Cup League 2** is a multi-year one-day international league for cricket's second tier of nations, running from 2023 to 2027. It's a key step on the qualification pathway toward the **2027 Cricket World Cup**, so results here have real stakes even though the teams involved — Scotland, Canada, Namibia, UAE, USA, and others — rarely make global headlines. Scotland and Canada have faced each other repeatedly in this cycle, most recently on August 7 in a tight 9-run Scotland win, and today's rematch in Dundee is part of the same tightly-fought race for qualification points.
stories.what_happened: Playing at their home ground of Forthill in Dundee, **Scotland batted first** against Canada in the 126th match of the League 2 cycle. At the time of writing, Scotland had reached **267/4**, with batter Michael Jones unbeaten on 41 and wicketkeeper Matthew Cross also not out, building a total aimed at extending their strong position near the top of the table. Scotland currently sit second in the League 2 standings with 38 points from 32 matches (16 wins), while Canada are fifth with 20 points from 20 games and need a strong finish to stay in contention for a World Cup Qualifier spot.
stories.why_it_matters: For cricket's smaller nations, League 2 matches like this one are often the difference between reaching a global tournament and missing out entirely — there's no broadcast deal or star-driven hype, but the competitive stakes for these teams' World Cup dreams are as real as any bigger series.
stories.ripple_effects: A strong Scotland performance here widens their cushion near the top of the table and pushes Canada further from a qualification spot, shaping the field that will eventually contest the 2027 World Cup Qualifier tournament.
stories.why_now: This is the second Scotland-Canada meeting inside a week as both teams pack in League 2 fixtures before the qualification window closes.
stories.watch_next: The final result of today's match, and how it shifts the League 2 points table with the qualification race intensifying.

key_terms.definition: A multi-year one-day international league among cricket's associate and lower-ranked nations that determines qualification paths to the Cricket World Cup.

stories.the_lesson: Sport's biggest stakes aren't always found in its biggest games — for teams outside cricket's traditional powers, a routine-looking league match can carry the same win-or-miss-the-World-Cup weight as a marquee fixture.

stories.title: Pakistan get a fitness boost as Shan Masood returns to training before the England Tests
key_points: Pakistan opener **Shan Masood** has returned to training, raising hopes he'll be fit for the first Test against England
Masood injured a finger during the opening Test of Pakistan's series against the **West Indies** in the Caribbean
He missed the second Test — which Pakistan still won, ending a **three-year wait** for an away Test victory
The Pakistan Test series against England begins **August 19 at Leeds**, with three Tests forming part of the 2025–2027 World Test Championship cycle
Pakistan currently sit **8th** in the World Test Championship standings, hoping this tour continues their recent resurgence
stories.background: Pakistan's Test team, now led by captain **Babar Azam**, has been in the middle of a tour of England that includes a three-day warm-up match against a Professional County Club Select XI before the main event: a **three-Test series** starting at Leeds on August 19, followed by Lord's and Birmingham. This series counts toward the **2025–2027 ICC World Test Championship**, the two-year league that determines which two teams reach the WTC final. Pakistan enter the tour off the back of a genuinely good result — beating the West Indies away for the first time in three years — but that win came with a cost: opening batter Shan Masood picked up a finger injury in the first Test of that series.
stories.what_happened: Masood, who missed the second Test of the West Indies series because of his finger injury, **resumed training with the Pakistan squad at Beckenham** this week, ahead of the team's three-day tour match there against a Professional County Club Select XI running August 13–15. His return to full training is being read as a positive sign for his availability for the first Test against England in Leeds on August 19. Pakistan's touring squad includes Babar Azam as captain, alongside Mohammad Rizwan, Saud Shakeel, Imam-ul-Haq, and a bowling attack featuring Mohammad Abbas, Aamir Jamal, and Sajid Khan.
stories.why_it_matters: Masood is one of Pakistan's most experienced Test openers, and having him fit to face the new ball against England's attack — especially at Leeds, a ground known for helping seam bowlers — materially improves Pakistan's chances in a series they'll want to use to build on their West Indies form.
stories.ripple_effects: A fit top order gives Pakistan a stronger platform against an England side under new Test captain Joe Root, who takes over from the retired Ben Stokes for this series — meaning both teams are carrying some uncertainty into the opener.
stories.why_now: Masood's return to training happened this week, directly ahead of Pakistan's final warm-up match before the Leeds Test begins.
stories.watch_next: Whether Masood is passed fit and included in Pakistan's XI for the first Test at Leeds on August 19.

key_terms.definition: A two-year league where all Test-playing nations play a set number of series against each other; the top two teams meet in a final to decide the overall Test champion.

stories.the_lesson: In Test cricket, a team's form often hinges as much on which players are fit to play as on raw skill — a single injured opener can change how an entire series is approached.

stories.title: India's injury crunch deepens: Sai Sudharsan ruled out of the Sri Lanka Tests with a toe fracture, and captain Shubman Gill is now under an injury cloud too

thread.previously: When India named its 15-man Test squad for Sri Lanka, Jadeja returned from injury but Jasprit Bumrah was ruled out; Sai Sudharsan and Bumrah's spots had been made conditional on fitness clearance, and Gill's own earlier finger injury was reported as resolved.
thread.changed: Sudharsan has now failed that fitness test and is officially ruled out with a toe stress fracture, with no replacement yet named — and captain Shubman Gill has picked up a new, separate injury, hurting his right ring finger in training in Colombo just before the series starts.

key_points: **Sai Sudharsan** is ruled out of the two-Test Sri Lanka series with a **toe stress fracture**.
He had been given a conditional spot pending fitness clearance from the BCCI's **Centre of Excellence (CoE)** — he didn't recover in time.
No replacement for Sudharsan has been named yet, and he did not travel with the squad to Sri Lanka.
Captain **Shubman Gill** is now also under an injury cloud after hurting his **right ring finger** in a training session in Colombo.
The series starts **August 15 in Galle**, with the second Test in **Colombo from August 23**.
stories.background: India named its Test squad for the Sri Lanka tour with some fitness question marks already attached: Sudharsan and Bumrah's places were both conditional on medical clearance after recent injuries, and Bumrah ultimately missed out. Sudharsan picked up a **toe stress fracture** — a small crack in the bone from repeated stress rather than a single impact — after returning from India A's tour of Sri Lanka in July, and had been at the BCCI's Centre of Excellence trying to recover in time.
stories.what_happened: India batter **Sai Sudharsan** has been ruled out of the upcoming two-Test series in Sri Lanka because of a **toe stress fracture** that hasn't healed enough for him to be declared fit. He had been named in the initial 15-man squad, but his selection — like Bumrah's — was conditional on medical clearance from the BCCI's Centre of Excellence, and he ultimately failed to get it in time; he did not travel with the squad and **no replacement has been named yet**. Adding to India's pre-series injury concerns, Test captain **Shubman Gill** is now also under an injury cloud after hurting his **right ring finger** during a training session in Colombo — a new issue, separate from an earlier finger problem that had already been reported resolved. The two-Test series begins **August 15 in Galle**, with the second Test starting **August 23** at the SSC in Colombo.
stories.why_it_matters: India already lost Bumrah, its premier fast bowler, to injury for this series, and now loses a top-order batting option too — while its own captain is battling a fresh knock just two days before the first ball, raising real questions about the depth and readiness of India's squad heading into a series against a Sri Lanka team playing at home.
stories.ripple_effects: Selectors will need to name a replacement batter quickly, likely reshaping India's top order for the series. If Gill's finger issue worsens, India could even face a late captaincy or personnel change right before the first Test, adding pressure on vice-captain KL Rahul to be ready to step in.
stories.why_now: The news broke just two days before the series opener on August 15, the point by which players' conditional fitness clearances had to be finalized one way or the other.
stories.watch_next: Whether India names a replacement for Sudharsan before the August 15 first Test, and whether Gill is passed fit to lead the side in Galle.

stories.the_lesson: Conditional squad selections — 'in the team pending fitness' — are a real risk, not a formality; when a team leans on several players clearing medical checks at once, injury depth becomes the deciding factor in how competitive the side actually is on day one.

stories.title: Bangladesh reach 96/1 at stumps, trailing Australia by just 102, after bowling the hosts out for 198
key_points: Bangladesh closed day one at **96/1**, trailing Australia's first-innings **198** by just **102 runs**.
**Mominul Haque and Tanzid Hasan** both finished the day not out, building a solid platform in reply.
Only **Mitchell Starc** looked genuinely threatening with the ball; the rest of Australia's attack, including Nathan Lyon, made little impact.
Bangladesh had earlier bowled Australia out for **198**, with **Hasan Mahmud** taking a career-best **6 for 55**.
It's Bangladesh's **first Test tour of Australia in 23 years** — and they've taken the early honours.
stories.background: Bangladesh arrived in Australia for their first Test tour of the country in 23 years, historically one of the toughest assignments in world cricket given Australia's pace-friendly home conditions. At Marrara Stadium in Darwin, Australia won the toss and chose to bat first — the conventional move at a ground where the pitch typically gets harder to bat on as a match wears on. Instead, Bangladesh's pace attack dismantled the Australian batting order on day one.
stories.what_happened: Australia were bowled out for just 198 on the opening day, with Hasan Mahmud claiming a career-best 6 for 55 — his third Test five-wicket haul — as Bangladesh's fast bowlers took all 10 Australian wickets, only the second time that has happened in the team's Test history. Steve Smith top-scored for the hosts with 71 off 109 balls. In reply, Bangladesh reached 96 for 1 by stumps, trailing by just 102 runs, with Mominul Haque and Tanzid Hasan both unbeaten and looking well set. Starc was the one Australian bowler who consistently troubled the Bangladesh batters, but the rest of the attack — including veteran spinner Nathan Lyon — couldn't find similar impact as conditions eased through the day.
stories.why_it_matters: A team on just its second-ever Test tour of Australia dominating day one of the series opener is a genuinely rare result — it flips the psychological pressure onto the home side and gives Bangladesh a real chance to post a first-innings lead in only their sixth Test match in the country.
stories.ripple_effects: A strong start here could reshape expectations for the rest of this historic two-Test series, with the second Test following at Mackay from August 22-26. It's also a significant confidence boost for Bangladesh's fast-bowling pipeline, led by the uncapped-to-star rise of Hasan Mahmud.
stories.why_now: This is the direct continuation of day one's play, with Bangladesh's reply innings unfolding through the same session in which they finished bowling Australia out.
stories.watch_next: Whether Mominul Haque and Tanzid Hasan can extend their partnership on day two and push Bangladesh into a first-innings lead against Australia at home.
stories.the_lesson: In cricket as in many contests, winning the toss and choosing the 'conventional' option isn't a guarantee — conditions and execution on the day can matter far more than the textbook strategy.

stories.title: Root scraps England's midnight curfew in his first move as reinstated Test captain
key_points: Joe Root has **abolished England's midnight curfew** ahead of the Pakistan Test series.
It's his **first concrete decision** since being reinstated as Test captain.
Root says players should be trusted to **manage themselves like adults** off the field, just as they are on it.

The three-match series against Pakistan begins **August 19**.
stories.background: England's Test set-up has been through turbulence this year: Ben Stokes retired in June during the New Zealand series, having earlier been suspended for a Test — along with pace bowler Gus Atkinson — for breaching the team's midnight curfew during a night out. Former coach Brendon McCullum also stepped down after England lost that series 2-1. Root, England's most-capped modern batter, has now returned to the Test captaincy he previously held, alongside a new coaching setup.
stories.what_happened: Root confirmed England will not operate under a curfew for the upcoming three-match Test series against Pakistan, arguing that if players are trusted to make good decisions on the field, they should be trusted to do the same off it. It's the first real decision of his reinstated captaincy, and directly reverses the disciplinary approach that led to Stokes and Atkinson's suspension earlier in the year. The series begins August 19.
stories.why_it_matters: It signals a deliberate cultural reset for an England dressing room that lost both its captain and its coach in the space of a few months — trading top-down discipline for personal responsibility right as a new leadership era begins.
stories.ripple_effects: The decision will be watched closely if England's on-field form or off-field discipline slips during the series — it sets an early tone for how the Root-Fleming era manages the team.
stories.why_now: It comes a week before the series opener, as Root settles into the captaincy and puts his own stamp on the team.
stories.watch_next: How England perform — and behave off the field — once the series against Pakistan starts on August 19.
stories.the_lesson: New leaders often reveal their approach first through small symbolic decisions — how a captain handles team culture says as much about their style as their tactics do.

stories.title: Hasan Mahmud's career-best 6-for stuns Australia as Bangladesh's pacers bowl them out for 198 in Darwin
key_points: Bangladesh bowled Australia out for just **198** on day one of the first Test in Darwin.
**Hasan Mahmud** took a career-best **6 for 55** — his third Test five-wicket haul.
Bangladesh's **fast bowlers took all 10 Australian wickets** — only the second time that's happened in the team's Test history.
**Steven Smith** top-scored for Australia with **71 off 109 balls**.
It's Bangladesh's **first Test tour of Australia in 23 years**.
stories.background: Bangladesh has not played a Test series in Australia in 23 years, making this tour a rare and significant assignment for a team more often associated with home conditions and spin bowling than fast bowling on the road. The first Test began August 13 at Marrara Stadium in Darwin and runs through August 17.
stories.what_happened: Australia won the toss and chose to bat first at Marrara Stadium in Darwin, but were bowled out for 198 by the end of the first day. Hasan Mahmud led the destruction with a career-best 6 for 55 — his third Test five-wicket haul — while Taskin Ahmed and Ebadot Hossain chipped in with two wickets each. It marked only the second time in Bangladesh's Test history that fast bowlers have taken all 10 wickets in an innings, after a similar feat in Rawalpindi in 2024. Steven Smith was the one bright spot for Australia, top-scoring with 71 off 109 balls including seven fours and a six.
stories.why_it_matters: This is a statement performance from a Bangladesh fast-bowling attack that has historically been considered the weaker part of its bowling arsenal compared to its spinners — and it came on just the first day of the team's first Test tour of Australia in over two decades.
stories.ripple_effects: A strong start with the ball puts pressure on Bangladesh's own batting lineup to make the most of it when they take strike, and could reshape how seriously opponents take Bangladesh's pace bowling on future away tours.
stories.why_now: It's day one of a five-day Test running through August 17, so this is just the opening chapter of the series — but a dominant one.
stories.watch_next: How Bangladesh's batters respond when they take strike, and whether the pace attack can back up this display for the rest of the match.

key_terms.definition: A bowler taking five or more wickets in a single innings — considered a standout individual bowling performance in cricket.

stories.the_lesson: Home advantage isn't automatic — a well-drilled bowling attack exploiting helpful conditions can undo even a strong batting lineup on its own turf.

stories.title: A record 231-run stand powers Afghanistan to a series-sealing 42-run win over Ireland

thread.previously: We reported Afghanistan had already secured a direct spot at the 2027 Cricket World Cup by beating Ireland in their ongoing ODI series.
thread.changed: Afghanistan has now won the 4th ODI too, by 42 runs, built on a record 231-run partnership between Ibrahim Zadran and Sediqullah Atal — extending their lead to an unassailable 3-0 with one match left.

key_points: Afghanistan beat Ireland by **42 runs** in the 4th ODI in Belfast, posting **343 for 9**.
**Ibrahim Zadran and Sediqullah Atal put on 231 runs** together — Afghanistan's highest-ever 2nd-wicket stand in ODIs.
**Sediqullah Atal scored 143** off 120 balls and was named Player of the Match.
Ireland fought back with **Andy Balbirnie (109)** and Curtis Campher (84), but fell short chasing 344.
The win gives Afghanistan an **unassailable 3-0 lead** in the five-match series, with one game left to play.
stories.background: Afghanistan's cricket team has become one of the format's most dangerous white-ball sides in recent years, built around explosive batting and world-class spin from players like Rashid Khan. This series in Ireland matters beyond bragging rights: Afghanistan had already used an earlier win in the series to lock in a direct qualification spot for the 2027 ODI Cricket World Cup, so these later matches are as much about form and momentum as they are about the series scoreline itself.
stories.what_happened: Afghanistan posted a commanding **343 for 9** in the 4th ODI at Belfast's Civil Service Cricket Club, anchored by a **231-run partnership** between **Ibrahim Zadran** and **Sediqullah Atal** — the highest second-wicket stand in Afghanistan's ODI history. Atal top-scored with **143 off 120 balls** and was named Player of the Match, while Ireland's McDonough (3 for 84) and Hoey (2 for 71) did what damage they could. Chasing 344, Ireland put up a real fight through half-centuries from **Andy Balbirnie (109)** and Curtis Campher (84), but fell 42 runs short, finishing on 301. Afghanistan's bowlers, led by **Yamin Ahmadzai (4 for 71)** and spin great **Rashid Khan (3 for 49)**, closed out the win. The result gives Afghanistan an **unassailable 3-0 lead** in the five-match series, with the fifth and final ODI still to come.
stories.why_it_matters: This isn't just a routine series win — Afghanistan piling up its highest-ever partnership for that wicket shows genuine batting depth developing behind its well-known bowling attack, which matters heading into a World Cup cycle where they've already qualified.
stories.ripple_effects: A dominant series like this builds momentum and confidence for Afghanistan ahead of the 2027 World Cup, and gives players like Atal a strong case for a settled middle-order spot. For Ireland, it's a tough series to take heading into their own World Cup qualification push, despite individual bright spots from Balbirnie and Campher.
stories.why_now: The 4th ODI was played on August 12, continuing a series that started earlier this month, with just the fifth and final match remaining.
stories.watch_next: The fifth and final ODI, where Ireland will look for a consolation win and Afghanistan will aim to complete a series whitewash.
stories.the_lesson: A single record partnership can change the entire shape of a match — big totals in limited-overs cricket usually trace back to one long stand where batters kept the scoreboard moving without losing wickets, rather than even scoring throughout the innings.

stories.title: Australia win the toss and bat first as the historic Bangladesh Test begins in Darwin

stories.title: Joe Root returns as England's Test captain for the Pakistan series, after Ben Stokes' shock retirement
key_points: England named a **16-player squad** for the first two Tests against Pakistan, with **Joe Root as captain** — his first time leading the side since **2022**.
Root steps in after **Ben Stokes' sudden retirement** from international cricket, announced mid-match during England's series against New Zealand.
**Jacob Bethell is ruled out** with a right knee injury; **Jordan Cox** is drafted in to bat at No. 3 in his place.
**Dan Lawrence and Ollie Pope** earn recalls to the squad as England rebuild for a **three-Test series starting August 19** at Headingley.
stories.background: Ben Stokes had captained England's Test side since 2022, reshaping the team around an aggressive, fast-scoring style known as "Bazball." His retirement mid-series against New Zealand stunned English cricket, ending a 15-year international career and leaving the captaincy vacant with a major home series against Pakistan just weeks away. Joe Root, England's most capped modern batter and their captain from 2017-2022 before he stepped down for Stokes, was the obvious experienced option to steady the side.
stories.what_happened: England's selectors have named Root as captain for at least the first two Tests of a three-match series against Pakistan, with reports suggesting he could stay in charge through next year's Ashes series if things go well. Alongside the captaincy change, the squad has been reshaped by injury and form: **Jacob Bethell**, tipped as a rising middle-order batter, is out with a knee injury, opening a spot for wicketkeeper-batter **Jordan Cox** to bat at No. 3. stories.why_it_matters: A captaincy change this close to a major series is a significant leadership reset for England's Test team, and how Root manages it will shape the team's identity after four years of Stokes' aggressive approach.
stories.ripple_effects: England's on-field strategy and team culture under Root may shift subtly from the Stokes era, while the recalled and injured players reshape the middle-order pecking order heading into a busy year that includes the Ashes. stories.why_now: Stokes' retirement was recent and sudden, so England had to settle the captaincy question quickly with the Pakistan series just over a week away when the squad was announced.
stories.watch_next: How Root's team performs and whether the ECB confirms him as captain beyond this series and into next year's Ashes.

stories.title: Australia bat first as Bangladesh's 23-year wait for a Test tour Down Under finally ends in Darwin
key_points: Australia won the toss and chose to **bat first** in the opening Test at **Marrara Cricket Ground, Darwin** — Bangladesh's **first Test tour of Australia in 23 years**.
It's also Darwin's **first Test match in 22 years**, played in **clear, sunny conditions around 31°C**.
Australia's XI features their full frontline pace attack — **Cummins, Starc and Hazlewood together** — plus Travis Head, Steven Smith and captain Pat Cummins.
Bangladesh arrive under pressure after being **bowled out for just 54** in their second innings of the warm-up match against a Cricket Australia XI.
stories.background: Bangladesh have toured Australia for Test cricket only rarely, and not at all in over two decades — a gap driven by scheduling, cricket-calendar priorities, and Australia's traditionally packed home summer. Darwin, in Australia's tropical Northern Territory, is an unusual and rarely-used Test venue, chosen partly to give Bangladesh conditions (heat, humidity) closer to what they're used to at home, even though the pitch and bounce still differ sharply from subcontinental cricket. Bangladesh's poor warm-up form has raised doubts about how competitive they can be against a full-strength Australian pace attack.
stories.what_happened: Play began today in Darwin with Australia's captain **Pat Cummins** winning the toss and electing to bat first, fielding a full-strength side: Travis Head, Jake Weatherald, Marnus Labuschagne, Steven Smith, Cameron Green, Alex Carey (wicketkeeper), Beau Webster, Cummins, **Mitchell Starc, Nathan Lyon and Josh Hazlewood** — reuniting Australia's premier pace trio of Cummins, Starc and Hazlewood for the first time in this series. Bangladesh, led by captain **Najmul Hossain Shanto**, have signalled they may field two spinners even on a fast, bouncy Australian pitch, after being dismissed for just 54 in their warm-up match's second innings. Weather forecasts point to dry, sunny conditions for all five days.
stories.why_it_matters: This is a genuine Test cricket rarity — a matchup and venue that essentially haven't happened in a generation — and an early gauge of whether Bangladesh's Test team can compete seriously outside home and familiar conditions against a full-strength opponent.
stories.ripple_effects: A heavy defeat would renew questions about Bangladesh's Test-match depth outside spin-friendly home pitches, while a competitive showing would boost their case for tougher future scheduling against top nations. For Australia, reuniting their first-choice pace attack is also a fitness and form checkpoint ahead of a busier home summer.
stories.why_now: The Test began today, August 13, as the first match of Bangladesh's tour, following their poor warm-up form which set the storyline for how the series opener would be watched.
stories.watch_next: Whether Bangladesh's bowling attack — potentially two spinners — can trouble Australia's top order, and how Bangladesh's batting responds after their warm-up collapse.

key_terms.definition: A coin flip before a cricket match; the winning captain chooses whether to bat or field first, a decision shaped heavily by pitch and weather conditions.

stories.the_lesson: In sport, a rarely-repeated fixture (a team's first tour to a place in decades) carries extra weight beyond the single result — it's often treated as a referendum on a team's overall growth, not just form on the day.

stories.title: South Africa hand Bjorn Fortuin the white-ball captaincy and blood fresh faces for a Namibia tour
